knowledge_graph.title: Cystinosis
knowledge_graph.description: Cystinosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by the abnormal accumulation of cystine, the oxidized dimer of the amino acid cysteine. It is a genetic disorder that follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy for cystinosis?
related_questions.snippet: Outlook / Prognosis At one point in time, nephropathic cystinosis was fatal in young children. Today, with the development of cysteamine and advancements in kidney transplantation, the life expectancy for people with cystinosis reaches far into adulthood. Some people live beyond 50 years of age.

related_questions.question: Can cystinosis be cured?
related_questions.snippet: Cystinosis can affect nearly every organ of the body. Cystinosis treatment can prevent or slow some effects, but existing damage cannot be reversed.

related_questions.question: What are the three types of cystinosis?
related_questions.snippet: There are three distinct types of cystinosis. In order of decreasing severity, they are nephropathic cystinosis, intermediate cystinosis, and non-nephropathic or ocular cystinosis.

text_blocks.snippet: Cystinosis is a rare, inherited metabolic disorder characterized by the buildup of cystine, an amino acid, within lysosomes (cellular compartments). This buildup damages various organs, particularly the kidneys and eyes. Cystinosis has three main forms: nephropathic (infantile and intermediate), and non-nephropathic (ocular). Nephropathic cystinosis, the most common and severe form, leads to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in childhood if left untreated.
snippet_highlighted_words: a rare, inherited metabolic disorder characterized by the buildup of cystine, an amino acid, within lysosomes (cellular compartments)

list.title: Cause:
list.snippet: A mutation in the CTNS gene impairs the function of the cystinosin protein, which normally transports cystine out of lysosomes.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms vary depending on the form of cystinosis but can include:
Nephropathic: Kidney problems (excessive urination, thirst, electrolyte imbalances, Fanconi syndrome), growth failure, photophobia (sensitivity to light), corneal crystals, and potentially ESRD.
Intermediate: Similar to nephropathic, but onset is later (adolescence).
Non-nephropathic (Ocular): Primarily photophobia and corneal crystals, with minimal or no kidney involvement.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Cystinosis is diagnosed by identifying symptoms, clinical evaluation, and specialized tests like measuring cystine levels in white blood cells and/or molecular genetic testing.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Cysteamine, a cystine-depleting medication, is the cornerstone of treatment, significantly delaying disease progression and improving outcomes. Treatment also addresses specific symptoms, such as thyroid hormone replacement or managing diabetes.

list.title: Prognosis:
list.snippet: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment with cysteamine are crucial for managing the disease and preventing complications. Untreated, nephropathic cystinosis can lead to ESRD, while the intermediate form may require transplant. Non-nephropathic cystinosis is generally considered benign.
